about: Two psalms, welded together. The question and the chalice come from Psalm 115; the last line, Laudans invocábo Dóminum, comes from Psalm 17. Cálicem salutáris accípiam is the verse the priest already borrowed once, before receiving the Host, with panem cæléstem put in place of the cup — now he says it as the psalm wrote it, with the chalice actually in his hand. Salutáris here is a noun, not an adjective: the chalice of salvation. The whole thing is said while he scrapes the paten clean over the chalice, so that not a fragment is lost; the psalm is set to a piece of housekeeping.

s01.narrative: The priest uncovers the chalice, genuflects, gathers any fragments and wipes the paten clean over the chalice, saying meanwhile:

s02.translation: What shall I render to the Lord for all that He has rendered to me?

s03.translation: I will take the chalice of salvation, and will call upon the name of the Lord.

s04.translation: With praise I will call upon the Lord, and I shall be saved from my enemies.

s05.narrative: He takes the chalice in his right hand and signs himself with it, saying:

s06.translation: May the Blood of our Lord Jesus Christ keep my soul unto life everlasting. Amen.

s07.narrative: Holding the paten beneath the chalice with his left hand, he reverently drinks all the Precious Blood together with the particle.

w001.function: Neuter accusative, the object of the verb that follows: an interrogative, though the same forms serve for the indefinite “someone, something” elsewhere.

w002.function: The corpus claims no tense and no mood here: the form is both the future indicative, “I shall render”, and the present subjunctive of deliberation, “what am I to render?”. Nothing in the sentence chooses, so nothing is claimed.

w006.function: Object of “retríbuit” (w007), not its subject: the things He rendered.

w007.function: Present and perfect are spelt alike in this verb; the perfect is read, because the benefits the question weighs are ones already given.

w008.function: The same verb both ways: what He rendered to me, and what I shall render to Him. The psalm turns the word round.

w010.function: A neuter noun in the genitive, salutáre, not the adjective salutáris that looks the same: the chalice belonging to salvation. Latin coined the noun to render a Greek one.

w011.function: Future indicative, as at the Host: “invocábo” (w015) beside it can only be future.

w016.function: A participle standing where English wants an adverb or a phrase: calling upon Him in the act of praising.

w023.function: With “ero” (w024) it forms the future of being safe, where English uses one word. Collatinus heads the word under its archaic nominative saluos, which is the same adjective; both analyzers read the form the same way.

w025.function: The form is the one said over the Host with a single word changed: Corpus there, Sanguis here, and nothing else.
